CausalChain: DDR gene mutations -> Accumulation of DNA damage -> Increased TMB and neoantigen load -> Activation of compensatory mechanisms including TGF-β signaling (with potential interaction with IFN-γ pathways) -> Upregulation of PD-L1 expression and recruitment of immunosuppressive cells -> Establishment of an immune 'cold' tumor microenvironment -> Reduced efficacy of ICIs
Hypothesis: In biliary tract cancers with DDR gene alterations, the resulting accumulation of DNA damage leads to a high TMB and neoantigen burden that not only primes the immune system but also triggers compensatory immunoregulatory pathways. We hypothesize that a key component of this compensatory response is the activation of TGF-β signaling, which, together with other cytokine-mediated signals (e.g., IFN-γ), drives enhanced PD-L1 expression and the recruitment of immunosuppressive cell populations. This cascade culminates in an immune 'cold' tumor microenvironment that diminishes the effectiveness of immune checkpoint inhibitors. Utilizing state-of-the-art CRISPR-based models, multi-omics analyses, and sophisticated in vivo imaging techniques, we propose that combined therapeutic inhibition of TGF-β and PD-L1 will overcome the immune resistance in this specific subset of BTC, thereby improving clinical outcomes.
Abstract: Biliary tract cancers (BTC) harboring DNA damage repair (DDR) gene alterations often exhibit genomic instability leading to a high tumor mutational burden (TMB) and an elevated neoantigen load. While such genomic alterations are anticipated to stimulate immune responses, emerging evidence suggests that compensatory mechanisms, notably TGF-β signaling activation, may concurrently drive PD-L1 upregulation and the recruitment of immunosuppressive cells. In this study, we propose that in a molecular subset of BTC with DDR defects, high TMB not only promotes neoantigen presentation but also triggers a multifaceted compensatory response wherein TGF-β signaling plays a crucial role. This pathway, possibly interacting with classical IFN-γ mediated mechanisms, contributes to the establishment of an immune ‘cold’ microenvironment, thus reducing the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). Leveraging contemporary technologies including CRISPR-engineered BTC models, high-dimensional multi-omics profiling, and advanced imaging of tumor-immune dynamics, we will assess whether dual inhibition of TGF-β and PD-L1 can counteract this compensatory immune resistance and thereby enhance ICI efficacy in DDR-altered BTC.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis linked DDR alterations to increased TMB which induces a compensatory activation of TGF-β signaling to upregulate PD-L1 and create an immunosuppressive microenvironment, thereby reducing ICI efficacy. In the revised hypothesis, we have explicitly acknowledged that while DDR alterations lead to high TMB and neoantigen production, there exists a broader set of compensatory immune regulatory responses that include, but are not limited to, TGF-β activation. We additionally recognize potential interactions with classical IFN-γ mediated pathways, thereby refining the causal chain. Furthermore, we have enhanced practical implementability by incorporating modern technological approaches such as CRISPR-engineered BTC models, advanced multi-omics profiling, and in vivo tumor-immune dynamics imaging to robustly validate the dual inhibition strategy of TGF-β and PD-L1. This integrated approach maintains the novelty and logical coherence of the original hypothesis while addressing key gaps and strengthening the translational potential of the therapeutic strategy.
